questions.stem: What does the resultant force describe?

options.text: The largest single force in the set
options.explanation: The resultant is not the maximum member; it is the combined effect of all of them.

options.text: The single force equivalent to all the forces acting together
options.explanation: It replaces the whole set with one net force.

options.text: The average of the force magnitudes
options.explanation: Averaging ignores which way each force points.

options.text: The force of friction only
options.explanation: Friction is one contributor, not the summary.

questions.stem: Two people push a crate from the same side with 30 N and 20 N. The resultant is:

options.text: 10 N, because forces always subtract
options.explanation: Subtraction is for opposing directions only.

options.text: 25 N, the mean of the two pushes
options.explanation: Averaging is not the combining law.

options.text: 50 N in the pushes' shared direction
options.explanation: Same-direction forces add: 30 + 20 = 50 N.

options.text: Zero, because the crate may not move
options.explanation: Motion is irrelevant; 50 N of resultant is present regardless.

questions.stem: Equal forces act in opposite directions on a bucket. The resultant is zero, and the forces are called:

options.text: Unbalanced
options.explanation: Unbalanced is precisely the opposite case.

options.text: Tension
options.explanation: Tension is a specific force, not this description.

options.text: Upthrust
options.explanation: Upthrust is a fluid's upward push.

options.text: Balanced
options.explanation: Equal opposing forces cancel: zero resultant, balanced pair.

questions.stem: A trolley feels 10 N to the right and 4 N to the left. Its resultant is:

options.text: 6 N to the right
options.explanation: 10 − 4 = 6 N, and the winner's side is the right.

options.text: 14 N to the right
options.explanation: Opposing forces subtract rather than add.

options.text: 6 N to the left
options.explanation: The larger force is the rightward one.

options.text: 4 N to the right
options.explanation: That ignores the 10 N force's full size.

questions.stem: Why must a resultant answer always name a direction?

options.text: Directions earn extra marks but carry no physics
options.explanation: The direction is physically essential, not decoration.

options.text: Because the magnitude changes if the direction is omitted
options.explanation: The magnitude is fixed by the arithmetic; it is the meaning that needs the direction.

options.text: Because examiners dislike bare numbers
options.explanation: The requirement is a law of the quantity, not a style rule.

options.text: Because forces are vectors: magnitude alone is an incomplete description
options.explanation: The same 6 N left and 6 N right are different physical situations.

questions.stem: State the two combining rules for forces that act along one line.
questions.modelAnswer: Forces pointing the same way add together; forces pointing in opposite directions subtract, and the resultant points the way of the larger side.

questions.stem: What is said about a set of forces that leaves no resultant on the body?
questions.modelAnswer: The forces are described as balanced: equal opposing effects that cancel completely.

questions.stem: Explain why the worked example's box ends up urged to the left.
questions.modelAnswer: The right-hand pushes total 4 + 8 = 12 N against a 14 N leftward force. Cancelling 12 of the 14 newtons leaves a 2 N surplus still pointing left, and that surplus is the resultant that urges the box leftwards.

questions.stem: A drawer sticks: you pull with 40 N while friction resists with 15 N. Give the resultant, with its direction.
questions.modelAnswer: 40 N − 15 N = 25 N, so the resultant force is 25 N in the pulling direction, and the drawer accelerates open.

questions.stem: Friction is defined as the force that:

options.text: Speeds objects up on rough ground
options.explanation: Friction never assists motion; it opposes it.

options.text: Opposes the motion of an object
options.explanation: This is the definition of record.

options.text: Acts only when objects are at rest
options.explanation: Sliding surfaces experience it precisely while moving.

options.text: Pulls objects towards the Earth
options.explanation: That describes weight, a different catalogue entry.

questions.stem: A box slides to the left across a floor. The friction force on the box points:

options.text: To the left, along with the motion
options.explanation: Friction opposes, never accompanies, the sliding.

options.text: It depends on the box's colour
options.explanation: Nothing about the sliding law depends on appearance.

options.text: To the right, against the sliding
options.explanation: Opposite to the motion means rightward here.

options.text: Downwards into the floor
options.explanation: The pressing contact is the reaction's job; friction lies along the surface.

questions.stem: At the microscopic level, friction exists because:

options.text: Surfaces are perfectly smooth and repel
options.explanation: Perfect smoothness would remove the catching, not cause it.

options.text: Both surfaces carry imperfections that push against each other
options.explanation: The imperfections catch — the cause of record.

options.text: Air pressure squeezes the surfaces together
options.explanation: Squeezing may press surfaces into contact, but the catching is the stated cause.

options.text: Magnetism in all materials
options.explanation: Magnetism is a separate catalogue entry.

questions.stem: Which statement about drag and air resistance is correct?

options.text: They are unrelated forces
options.explanation: Air resistance is a special case of drag.

options.text: Drag acts only in liquids
options.explanation: Gases are fluids too; drag covers both.

options.text: Air resistance pushes objects forward
options.explanation: Like all friction, it opposes the motion.

options.text: Air resistance is the drag special case for motion through air
options.explanation: Drag covers fluids generally — liquids and gases; air resistance is its air case.

questions.stem: A sledge slides down a snowy slope. The friction from the snow on the sledge acts:

options.text: Up the slope, against the sliding
options.explanation: Opposite to the motion means back up the slope.

options.text: Down the slope, helping the slide
options.explanation: Friction never helps the sliding.

options.text: Vertically upwards only
options.explanation: Friction lies along the contacting surfaces, here the slope's line.

options.text: Sideways off the slope
options.explanation: Nothing turns the friction sideways here.

questions.modelAnswer: Friction is the force that opposes the motion of an object, arising where surfaces rub against each other.

questions.stem: Name the frictional force on an object moving through air, and the general name for any fluid.
questions.modelAnswer: In air the force is air resistance; the general fluid case is called drag.

questions.stem: Explain why the same crate is harder to drag across a rough carpet than a smooth floor.
questions.modelAnswer: The carpet's surface carries larger imperfections, so more catching occurs where the crate slides. More catching means a larger frictional force opposing the motion, which is why the same push moves the crate less easily on the carpet.

questions.stem: A sledge is hauled along a frozen path with 60 N while snow friction opposes it with 15 N. Give the resultant and its direction.
questions.modelAnswer: 60 N − 15 N = 45 N, so the resultant is 45 N forwards along the path — the sledge speeds up in that direction.
